description: Hey there! We are an enthusiastic team teaming up for NASA's "Be An Earth System Trend Detective" challenge. Bringing together a shared passion for environmental science, data, and AI, we love connecting real-world ecological curiosity with smart data exploration to see how our planet is changing. We are all about good teamwork, learning together, and turning complex Earth observations into exciting discoveries!
summary:
TerraPulse is a web app that turns NASA Earth observation data into explanations of environmental change. Users select a place and explore vegetation greenness (MODIS NDVI), daytime land surface temperature (MODIS), rainfall (GPM IMERG), or nitrogen dioxide air pollution (OMI). An interactive map shows how results differ across locations.
TerraPulse builds and checks time series, then uses the seasonal Mann-Kendall test to identify significant trends and Sen's slope to measure their rate of change with a 95% range. It accounts for seasonal patterns, guards against false findings when testing many cells, and reports when evidence is insufficient. To avoid a false cooling trend caused by Terra's earlier overpass time since 2020, the daytime temperature analysis ends in December 2021. The method found 28 of 28 planted trends in simulated data and agreed with an Alexandria ground weather station on warming. Results include New Delta greening of about +0.039 NDVI per decade since 2001 and Nile Delta land surface warming of about 0.4 °C per decade from 2001 to 2021.
TerraPulse makes Earth science understandable without programming or statistics skills. Kemet, its English- and Arabic-speaking AI guide, uses only TerraPulse's computed numbers and documented facts to explain results without inventing causes.
details:
Is the Nile Delta really changing, and can you prove it?
New farmland is spreading into the desert of the New Delta. Vegetation around Alexandria is declining. The air over Greater Cairo carries more nitrogen dioxide than it did twenty years ago. NASA satellites have recorded all of this for decades, but turning those records into an answer you can trust takes data and statistics skills most people do not have. TerraPulse closes that gap: pick a place and a variable, and it tells you what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. When the evidence is not there, it says so.

What it does and how it works
TerraPulse is a web app that investigates environmental change using NASA Earth observation data. Users select a variable and location; TerraPulse builds a time series (measurements over time), measures the rate of change and tests whether a trend is statistically significant.
It covers four variables:
- Vegetation greenness (MODIS Terra NDVI, monthly, 1 km)
- Daytime land surface temperature (MODIS Terra, 1 km)
- Rainfall (GPM IMERG monthly)
- Nitrogen dioxide air pollution (Aura OMI)
A NOAA weather station in Alexandria provides an independent ground check. Users can select preset regions, click a single map cell of about 5 km, or draw a box for live analysis.
MODIS data comes through NASA AppEEARS, GPM IMERG and OMI area averages through NASA Giovanni, and weather records from NOAA. TerraPulse removes fill values, applies scale factors and quality flags, drops impossible values and spikes, and calculates monthly averages. Missing data is never invented. The 1 km grids are averaged into about 5 km cells (2,520 cells over the Nile Delta).
NASA's Terra satellite stopped correcting its orbit in 2020, causing daytime temperatures to read cooler each year. To avoid a false cooling trend, temperature analysis ends at December 2021.
The seasonal Mann-Kendall test compares the same months across years, so seasonal cycles are not mistaken for trends, while Sen's slope measures the rate of change with a 95% range. Benjamini-Hochberg q-values correct for false discoveries across hundreds of cells.
Results receive clear verdicts: confirmed trend, possible trend, real but too small to matter, no significant trend, or not enough data (records shorter than 10 years). Interactive maps, charts and an Evidence tab display results and explain p-values, q-values and the 95% range.

Evidence tab: how strong the evidence is, the 95% range compared with "no change", the seasonal Mann-Kendall p-value and the Benjamini-Hochberg q-value, each explained in plain words.

Try it in under a minute
1. Choose a variable, for example vegetation greenness.
2. Pick a preset region such as the New Delta, click any 5 km map cell, or draw your own box on the map.
3. Read the verdict on the Overview tab, see the time series and trend on the Trend tab, and check the p-value, q-value and 95% range on the Evidence tab, each explained in plain words.
4. Ask Kemet, the AI guide, what the result means, in English or Arabic.
A guided tour and a narrated walkthrough video help first-time users.

TerraPulse home screen: start exploring Earth's environmental changes or take the platform tour.

How we know it works
- Planted-trend test: on simulated data with planted trends, TerraPulse found 28 of 28 planted trend cells, with 1 false alarm in 89 no-trend cells.
- Ground check: the Alexandria weather station warmed about 0.60 °C per decade (2000-2023; a separate ground record, not affected by the satellite cutoff), compared with MODIS land surface warming there of about 0.51 °C per decade (2001-2021). This independent ground-based check agrees with the satellite on the direction of warming.

What TerraPulse found
- New Delta greening: about +0.039 NDVI per decade since 2001 (p < 0.001).
- Alexandria browning: about -0.038 NDVI per decade.
- Nile Delta land surface warming: about 0.40 °C per decade from 2001 to 2021.
- Greater Cairo: rising nitrogen dioxide since 2004.
- Rainfall: no significant trend in the Nile Delta, on the Mediterranean coast, or in the Central Amazon (1998-2025). TerraPulse treats this as a meaningful finding, not a failure.

Overview tab: the New Delta verdict, "Trend confirmed by the evidence", at +0.039 NDVI per decade (95% range +0.035 to +0.044). Map cells are coloured by their verdict.

Trend tab: the New Delta (greening) and Alexandria (browning) side by side, using yearly averages and trend lines on the same scale.

Benefits
- Students and teachers can explore NASA data and learn what "significant" means without programming or statistics skills.
- The public can check environmental change against evidence in English or Arabic, with simple variable definitions and clear uncertainty reporting that prevents unsupported conclusions.
- Researchers and analysts save hours of data preparation and analysis and get a transparent first look at trends, with the uncertainty shown.

Intended impact
TerraPulse helps people understand environmental changes through evidence, particularly vegetation, surface heat and air quality in Egypt. It highlights changes such as new farmland in the New Delta, browning around Alexandria and rising air pollution over Cairo. It also treats the absence of a significant trend as a meaningful finding.

What makes it creative
Kemet takes its name from the ancient name of Egypt, meaning "the Black Land", referring to the Nile's fertile soil. It uses only TerraPulse's computed numbers and documented facts about each place, never inventing causes. Every answer names the model that wrote it. Everyday verdicts distinguish statistical significance from practical importance. Users can draw a box for a full trend test in seconds. The "Oasis" colour palette reflects the Nile's land, water and palm trees, while ground weather observations provide an independent satellite check.

Kemet, the AI guide, answering "Why might this happen?" in English (Arabic is one click away). The answer names the model that wrote it and uses only the numbers TerraPulse computed.

Factors we considered
We considered data quality, sensor orbit drift, seasonal cycles and false discoveries. Without correction, about 5% of cells could appear significant by chance. Records shorter than 10 years are labelled "not enough data", while changes smaller than the instrument's uncertainty are labelled "real but tiny". TerraPulse and Kemet avoid unsupported explanations of causes. We prioritised simple language and two languages for the challenge's high school and college students and the public. Everything uses free NASA data, free and open-source software, and free AI models, so the tool costs nothing to run.

Scalability and future possibilities
TerraPulse's method is not tied to one place or one variable, making it adaptable to a wider range of environmental studies. Its potential for expansion includes:
- Anywhere on Earth: The same analysis workflow can be applied to new regions worldwide by defining an area, obtaining the relevant NASA Earth observation data and running the existing analysis steps.
- More of the Earth system: Extending the methodology to additional variables, such as soil moisture and evaporation, alongside vegetation greenness, land surface temperature, rainfall and nitrogen dioxide.
- From trends to outlooks: Exploring forecasting approaches built on historical trend evidence, with uncertainty clearly communicated and predictions independently validated.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)
We used SI tools in three clearly labelled ways:
- Kemet, the in-app guide: NVIDIA Nemotron language models through OpenRouter. Kemet receives only the numbers TerraPulse computed and a short list of documented facts about each place, and names the model behind every answer. It explains results; it does not calculate, determine or produce them, and the Overview, Trend and Evidence tabs always remain the reference.
- Coding assistant: Claude by Anthropic, used for code, interface design and documentation.
- Video narration: Kokoro text-to-speech, labelled as AI-generated in the videos.
All trend results, statistics and validation numbers come from TerraPulse's own analysis code running on NASA and NOAA data, not from an AI model. No SI-generated content uses NASA logos or branding.

Tools and technologies
- Data: NASA AppEEARS, Giovanni (Earthdata Login) and NOAA Climate Data Online.
- Analysis: Python, pandas, xarray, NumPy, SciPy, netCDF4 and pymannkendall.
- Web: FastAPI, JavaScript, Leaflet, Leaflet.draw, Plotly.js and Esri World Imagery.
- AI: NVIDIA Nemotron language models through OpenRouter (Kemet); Claude by Anthropic (coding assistant for code, interface design and documentation); Kokoro text-to-speech (video narration, labelled as AI-generated).
- Hosting and code: Vercel and GitHub.
No special hardware is needed; everything runs in a web browser.
